subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on chemical changes, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain chemical changes for GCSE simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Acids, alkalis, the pH scale and indicators
Neutralisation and strong and weak acids
Reactions of acids to make salts
Electrolysis of molten and aqueous compounds
The reactivity series and extraction of metals

questions.lo: Acids, alkalis, the pH scale and indicators
questions.q: Which ion is present in all acidic solutions?
questions.explain: Acids release hydrogen ions, H+, in aqueous solution. Alkalis release hydroxide ions, OH-.

questions.lo: Acids, alkalis, the pH scale and indicators
questions.q: A solution has a pH of 12. Which colour would universal indicator turn and what is the solution?
questions.explain: A pH of 12 is alkaline. Universal indicator turns purple/blue in alkaline solutions. pH 7 is green (neutral) and low pH is red (acidic).

questions.lo: Acids, alkalis, the pH scale and indicators
questions.q: What colour is litmus in an alkaline solution?
questions.explain: Litmus is blue in alkali and red in acid.

questions.lo: Neutralisation and strong and weak acids
questions.q: What is always produced when an acid neutralises an alkali?
questions.explain: Neutralisation of an acid by an alkali produces a salt and water. The ionic equation is H+ + OH- gives H2O.

questions.lo: Neutralisation and strong and weak acids
questions.q: A strong acid and a weak acid have the same concentration. Why does the strong acid have the lower pH?
options: It is fully (completely) ionised, releasing more H+
questions.explain: A strong acid is completely ionised in water, releasing more H+ ions, so it has a lower pH than a weak acid of the same concentration, which is only partially ionised.

questions.lo: Neutralisation and strong and weak acids
questions.q: As the H+ concentration of an acid increases by a factor of 10, how does the pH change?
questions.explain: The pH scale is logarithmic. A tenfold increase in H+ concentration lowers the pH by 1 unit.

questions.lo: Reactions of acids to make salts
questions.q: Acid + metal carbonate produces which set of products?
questions.explain: Acid reacting with a metal carbonate produces a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

questions.lo: Reactions of acids to make salts
questions.q: Which salt is produced when magnesium reacts with sulfuric acid?
questions.explain: Sulfuric acid produces sulfate salts, so magnesium + sulfuric acid gives magnesium sulfate and hydrogen.

questions.lo: Reactions of acids to make salts
questions.q: Acid + metal oxide (a base) produces which products?
questions.explain: A metal oxide is a base; acid + metal oxide gives a salt and water.

questions.lo: Making soluble and insoluble salts
questions.q: To make a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble base, what do you do with the excess base?
options: Leave it dissolved in the solution
Boil it away with the water
Add more acid to dissolve it
questions.explain: Excess insoluble base is added to ensure all the acid reacts, then the unreacted excess is filtered off before the solution is crystallised to give the pure salt.

questions.lo: Making soluble and insoluble salts
questions.q: Insoluble salts are usually made by which method?
questions.explain: Insoluble salts are made by precipitation: mixing two solutions of soluble compounds so the insoluble salt forms as a precipitate, which is then filtered, washed and dried.

questions.lo: Electrolysis of molten and aqueous compounds
questions.q: During electrolysis, to which electrode do positive ions (cations) move?
questions.explain: Positive ions (cations) are attracted to the cathode, the negative electrode, where they gain electrons (reduction).

questions.lo: Electrolysis of molten and aqueous compounds
questions.q: When molten lead bromide is electrolysed, what forms at the cathode?
questions.explain: In molten lead bromide, lead ions are reduced at the cathode to form lead metal, while bromine forms at the anode.

questions.lo: Electrolysis of molten and aqueous compounds
questions.q: During the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (brine), which gas is produced at the anode?
questions.explain: Electrolysis of concentrated brine produces chlorine at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode, and leaves sodium hydroxide solution.

questions.lo: Electrolysis of molten and aqueous compounds
questions.q: Which half-equation correctly shows the reaction at the cathode when hydrogen is produced?
questions.explain: At the cathode, hydrogen ions gain electrons (reduction): 2H+ + 2e- gives H2. Losing electrons occurs at the anode.

questions.lo: The reactivity series and extraction of metals
questions.q: A metal is found in the Earth as its oxide and is extracted by reduction with carbon. Where is this metal in the reactivity series?
options: It is an unreactive noble gas
questions.explain: Metals less reactive than carbon (such as iron and zinc) can be extracted by reduction with carbon. Metals more reactive than carbon are extracted by electrolysis.

questions.lo: The reactivity series and extraction of metals
questions.q: Which metal is extracted by electrolysis because it is too reactive to be reduced by carbon?
questions.explain: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so it is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide rather than reduction with carbon.

questions.lo: The reactivity series and extraction of metals
questions.q: Zinc is placed in copper sulfate solution. What happens?
options: Zinc displaces copper because zinc is more reactive
No reaction, zinc is less reactive
questions.explain: Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper sulfate solution, forming zinc sulfate and copper metal (the blue colour fades).

questions.lo: Oxidation and reduction (OIL RIG)
questions.q: In terms of electrons, what is oxidation?
questions.explain: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.

questions.lo: Oxidation and reduction (OIL RIG)
questions.q: In the reaction Zn + Cu2+ gives Zn2+ + Cu, which species is reduced?
questions.explain: Cu2+ gains electrons to become Cu, so it is reduced (RIG). Zn loses electrons to become Zn2+, so it is oxidised.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9–1) Chemistry (1CH0) specification; Chemical Changes
